chunks: 5493 - Al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb narrated from Abū Jamīlah, from Ḥumrān, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام:

Concerning a man who made a bequest at the time of his death and said: 'Free so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so,' until he mentioned five. Then his one-third was examined, but his one-third did not reach the prices of the value of the five slaves whom he ordered to be freed.

He عليه السلام said: 'The ones whom he named are to be considered in the order he named them and began with freeing them. They are to be appraised, and his one-third is considered; then the first thing he mentioned is freed from it, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, then the fifth. If the one-third falls short, it applies to the one he named last, because he ordered emancipation beyond the amount of the one-third with what he does not own, so that is not permissible for him.'

key_terms.الْمَمَالِيكِ: the slaves owned by the deceased
key_terms.ثُلُثِهِ: the one-third portion of the estate that may be disposed of by will

ai.seo_question: If a dying person orders several slaves to be freed but his one-third of the estate is insufficient, which of them are freed first?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling about a deathbed bequest for the emancipation of slaves when the deceased's one-third share is insufficient to cover all those named. The named slaves are freed in the exact order mentioned, and once the one-third is exhausted, the later ones are not included because a bequest cannot validly exceed the testator's lawful disposable third.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.5493 - Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Abu Jamilah from Humran from Abu Jafar Imam Muhammad ibn Ali Al-Baqir (as)

regarding a man who, on his deathbed, made a will saying, "Free so-and-so, and so-and-so, and so-and-so," until he mentioned five individuals. When his estate was assessed, it was found that one-third of his wealth was not enough to cover the value of the five slaves he had ordered to be freed.

Imam (as) said: "The individuals he named should be evaluated according to their order of mention, starting with the first. They should be valued, and their emancipation should proceed from the first he mentioned, then the second, the third, the fourth, and finally the fifth. If the one-third of the estate runs out before reaching the last, then the last named does not get freed because the man ordered their emancipation beyond the limit of what he lawfully owned, and thus it is not permissible."
